articles.title: Chapter Notes: October 2026
articles.author: Pinellas DSA
articles.content: We recruited the 400th member of Pinellas DSA this month — and we’re still growing! BOO, comrade! An extra-spooky Halloween edition of the Pinellas DSA newsletter is here! We hit another exciting milestone in September — our chapter is now officially more than 400 members strong! That’s 400 friends and neighbors who’ve made the choice to stand up and say “I believe that a better world is possible.” And, as long as we keep doing the day-to-day work of building our organization and growing the international movement for socialism, we will transform possible into inevitable . Read on to learn more about what our chapter was up to over the last month, and what we have coming up next! September Highlights PDSA comrades at the September Interest Meeting & New Member Orientation. September was a month of steady progress for our ongoing campaigns. Perhaps the biggest development came early in the month when DSA comrades behind the Dump Duke campaign held a press conference in Williams Park to announce the launch of a petition campaign to place an amendment for public power on the 2028 ballot. Meanwhile, organizers behind the No on 3 initiative wasted no time, launching a series of door-to-door canvasses, lit drops, and more to get the word out about the threat Amendment 3 poses to our communities. We also established a social media presence for our DeFlock St. Pete campaign, which has already seen a major win with a new business item in front of the St. Pete City Council, introduced by Councilmember and DSA comrade Richie Floyd, to allow for the discussion of the city’s Flock contract. We also published the first in a fantastic new series of videos from our International Solidarity Working Group, with the aim of educating the masses on the legacy of US imperialism in the Caribbean. Check it out on the official Pinellas DSA YouTube channel (and subscribe while you’re at it)! Lastly, we want to also spotlight the Pinellas DSA blog , which is where you can find updates and official statements published on behalf of the chapter. We’re also accepting submissions for the blog from any active member in good standing; email us at dsa.pinellas@gmail.com if you’d like to pitch your article! CAMPAIGN UPDATE: Dump Duke On September 2, Pinellas DSA members held a press conference to announce the launch of a petition campaign to place a charter amendment on the 2028 ballot. If successful, the initiative would give St. Pete voters the opportunity to decide whether the city should establish a publicly owned electric utility. The event, which was held in Williams Park — directly across the street from Duke Energy headquarters — was also the official launch of Public Power St. Pete, a coalition aimed at advancing the #DumpDuke mission. Besides Pinellas DSA, other coalition members include the CLEO Institute, Sierra Club Suncoast Group, Florida Youth Action Fund, People Power for Florida, and Florida Rising. At the heart of this campaign is a simple goal: making electricity more affordable, reliable, and locally controlled for St. Pete residents. It won’t be easy, though: organizers will need to collect 16,200 petitions with verified signatures from St. Pete voters, with the aim to secure over 20,000 signatures. Learn more about the petition drive here CAMPAIGN UPDATE: DeFlock St. Pete As mentioned above, Councilmember Richie Floyd introducing a business item during a meeting of the St. Pete City Council at the end of August to allow for the discussion of the city’s Flock contract. Specifically, how we can eliminate it . You might reasonably assume that this initiative would see pushback from at least a few of the council’s more conservative members. However, St. Pete City Council voted unanimously to pass this item, and advance the discussion to the city’s Public Services & Infrastructure Committee. Richie sits on the committee, as do Councilmembers Hanewicz, Harting, and Gerdes. Organizers with the DeFlock St. Pete campaign are asking anyone who is “passionate about preventing our little slice of Florida from becoming part of the surveillance state” to reach out to the three committee members in question, thank them for backing Richie’s business item, and let them know that you want to #DeFlockStPete! You can reach the officials in question using the contact information provided below: Copley Gerdes: copley.gerdes@stpete.org | (727) 551–3528 Mike Harting: mike.harting@stpete.org | (727) 551–3305 Lisset Hanewicz: lisset.hanewicz@stpete.org | (727) 893–7412 CAMPAIGN UPDATE: No on 3 PDSA comrades out knocking doors to get out the vote against Amendment 3. Organizers behind the No on 3 campaign hit the ground running last month, launching into a series of door-to-door canvasses, lit drops, and “public service stakeouts” to rally Pinellas residents to defeat Amendment 3 on the November ballot. If Amendment 3 passes, Pinellas County residents will suffer from millions of dollars in public funding cuts each year, impacting EMS, fire and rescue, flood mitigation, infrastructure repair, libraries, parks, public transit, and more. This campaign was spun up on short notice, withe less than three months to get the word out. But, organizers have done a phenomenal job so far! articles.title: Interest Rate Increases Are About Disciplining Labor
articles.author: Arthur MacEwan
articles.content: Using its favored policy in the face of inflation, the Federal Reserve Board, under its new chairman, Kevin Warsh, pushed up short-term interest rates in September. This action may have some impact on the rate of inflation, but probably not much. Raising interest rates may curtail inflation under some circumstances, but the major factors bringing about the current, continuing inflation are unlikely to be much affected by the Fed’s recent interest rate increases. But those other factors are out of bounds: the Fed can’t alter them, and the current administration in Washington won’t. What Washington Has Done to Curtail Inflation With the emergence of economic instability in the early 1970s, President Richard Nixon imposed wage-price controls that limited how much wages and prices could rise. To oversee wage-price controls, his administration established two agencies, a Pay Board and a Cost of Living Council. Economist Arnold Weber was the executive director of the Cost of Living Council and a member of the Pay Board. In 1974, Weber summed up the actions that these federal institutions had undertaken to contain inflation with this statement , “The goal here is to zap labor. That’s what we’re doing here. . . . We have to zap labor.” Attempting to quell inflation in 2022 by pushing interest rates up, then–Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board Jerome Powell saw the problem this way : “ . . . look at the average hourly earnings number we got with the last payrolls report. You don’t really see much progress in terms of average hourly earnings coming down.” Whether the mechanism was wage-price controls, raising interest rates, zapping labor, or, as Powell proclaimed, viewing “progress in terms of average hourly earnings coming down,” the authorities in Washington have been consistent in the way they have seen policy bringing about a reduction of inflation. Since the 1970s, the favored mechanism has been for the Fed to raise interest rates. The rationale is simple: raising interest rates makes it more costly to borrow money, and this leads both businesses and households to hold off on spending (fewer new factories, reduced housing construction, and fewer car purchases, for example). This reduction in investment lessens hiring and costs some workers their jobs. That in turn weakens the bargaining power of workers, leading to lower wages, or at least slower wage increases. As the wage bill of employers (how much employers spend on labor) grows more slowly and the buying power of workers ebbs, prices will tend to fall, or at least not rise so rapidly. This policy has its greatest impact on workers, many of whom lose their jobs, and almost all are in a weaker position to attain wage gains. Yes, businesses can be hurt too in these circumstances. Yet for those who make the policies, the primary problem is that wages are getting out of hand, and it is workers who will bear the burden of the policy. Moreover, the impact on labor tends to have the long-run effect of weakening the power of workers. The most dramatic application of this anti-inflation policy took place in the early 1980s. Prices, as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), rose at an annual rate of more than 10 percent between mid-1977 and mid-1981. By the middle of 1981, the Fed had pushed up the Federal Funds Effective Rate (FFER) to over 20 percent, and that rate did not fall below 10 percent until August 1982. (The FFER is the interest rate banks charge on overnight loans to each other, and it is the rate most immediately affected by Fed actions.) It worked. Inflation abated, running at an annual rate of less than 3 percent in the mid-1980s. And unemployment? The unemployment rate rose to 10.8 percent at the end of 1982, the highest monthly rate since World War II, except for some months during the pandemic of the early 2020s. And wages? The average wages for all workers fell off between the 1970s and 1980, and, for workers in the bottom half (by wage level) of the labor force, it wasn’t until the mid-1990s that wages again reached the level of the 1970s. Labor had been zapped. So why won’t it work this time? Causes of the Current Inflation Higher interest rates tend to stop or slow inflation by reducing aggregate demand — that is, overall spending in the economy — thus curtailing employment, pushing wages down, and thereby reducing inflation. However, it is hard to blame wages for the current inflation when labor costs have not been rising as fast as prices. The Financial Times reports that the rate of labor costs per unit of output — that is, the labor cost of producing a given amount of goods and services — “over the last four years has averaged 2 percent and during the past year is running at 1.5 percent,” both of which are less than the rate of inflation. And, according to The Financial Times , “over the last 12 months, average hourly earnings have risen at the slowest pace in seven years.” Furthermore, the share of national output going to labor — that is, the portion of the economy’s income paid to workers — is lower than at any time since World War II, having fallen from between 61 percent and 66 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1960s to 53 percent of GDP today. In any case, important causes of the current inflation are not demand problems. Some are instead supply problems — shortages or higher costs that limit the amount of goods and services available — that have followed from the perverse policies of the Trump administration: The war that the United States initiated against Iran has had severe impacts on the price of oil and oil-based products (especially fertilizer). The high price of oil feeds through the whole economy, as is starkly seen in the way the price of diesel fuel, which was $6.51 per gallon in late September, has affected the cost of transporting goods. The Trump administration’s imposition of tariffs has had an across-the-board impact on prices. Not only are the prices of the imported goods themselves raised, but much of what the United States imports is used as an input for domestically produced goods — automobiles are a well-known and important example. A less well-known example was pointed out in 2021 by The Economist : “Pfizer’s [covid] vaccine requires 280 inputs from suppliers in 19 countries. No firm can recreate that in a hurry.” Because complex international supply chains cannot be changed quickly, tariffs tend to push up the costs of many goods that are not directly affected by the tariffs. The massive campaign by the Trump administration to push immigrants out of the country has led to significant labor shortages in several industries — construction, meatpacking, and agriculture are all examples. According to the White House , “The Trump administration has deported more than 605,000 illegal aliens, with an additional 1.9 million self-deporting, bringing the total number of illegals who have left the U.S. since President Trump returned to office to over 2.5 million.” Labor supply shortages tend to push up prices. Not all of the factors bringing about the recent inflation are on the supply side. Yet two important demand factors are unlikely to be substantially affected by the Fed’s effort to push up interest rates. One of these factors is the large government deficit, a consequence of large tax reductions for the wealthy without a matching decrease of spending — as cuts to programs for the poor have been offset by increases in military spending. (Not only has the Republican congress legislated tax reductions, especially for the wealthy, but there is also the failure of the IRS to halt tax evasion.) It is possible, of course, that higher interest rates, which are also increasing the costs of government debt payments, might bring some sanity to the federal budget, but this seems unlikely. Moreover, interest rates on Treasury bonds, the cost of government debt payments, are already higher than at any time in the last two decades. The other demand factor contributing to inflation is the enormous investment in data centers being constructed to support artificial intelligence. These data centers are leading to electricity price increases in several parts of the country, and the expenditure on their construction is keeping aggregate demand strong. Of course, much of the expenditures on data centers is financed by debt, and the taking on of debt might be reduced by rising interest rates. But it seems that companies such as Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet (Google) are unlikely to substantially slow their activity because of interest rate hikes. For them, artificial intelligence promises the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. The Trump administration is very unlikely to cease its military actions in the Middle East (and elsewhere), to abandon the tariffs, or to stop pushing people out of the country — all of which affect prices by disruption of supply. And the government deficit and the massive expenditures on data centers are unlikely to be seriously affected by the Fed’s action on interest rates. So, when all else is out of bounds, zap labor. An Afterword I cannot help but comment on the irony that, while progressive economists have long been critical of, and generally opposed to, the Fed using rate hikes to quell inflation, today it is President Donald Trump who is doing so with his rants for lower interest rates. I can defend those of us on the Left by pointing out that we have opposed the supply-related policies noted above — the military actions, the inane tariffs, and the expulsion of people who have come here to work (and who pay taxes). Also, we have opposed the tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending that have fueled the inflation, and we are not at all happy with the push to build data centers. Dealing with these issues could reduce inflation without zapping labor (though electricians working on the data centers might object). Trump, however, seems oblivious to even the existence of an inflation problem and its severe effects on the cost of living. He seems to think that the important issue is keeping interest rates low as a means of pushing economic growth and keeping the stock market booming. It appears, however, that inflation has more people (voters) agitated than slow economic growth or a possible stock market slump. But while I may be able to explain why progressive economists think the way we do, I make no attempt to explain the president’s thinking! articles.title: Why Organize Semiconductor Workers? w/ CHIPS Communities United
articles.content: Block & Build is a weekly newsmagazine podcast from Convergence Magazine that examines the balance of political forces in the US from a movement perspective. Every week, host Cayden Mak explores what's… This is the last article. Subscribe to our email newsletter to get more. Semiconductors are at the heart of every piece of electronics you interact with on a daily basis. Despite being invented and innovated in the US, much of the manufacturing of semiconductors and the technology they power was “offshored” from the 1980s through the early 2000s as part of the globalization of our economy. In an effort to counter that loss of jobs and industry, the Biden administration passed the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, which reinvests over $50 billion domestically in the manufacturing and research of semiconductors in the United States. While this has started to proffer new work opportunities and industrial development in the US, workers in the industry are organizing for wall-to-wall unions in their facilities as well as better conditions for the communities that house them. The result of that organizing is CHIPS Communities United , a coalition organizing for an equitable and sustainable semiconductor manufacturing industry. Their alliance includes labor, environmental, social justice, civil rights, and community organizations representing millions of workers and community members nationwide. Their vision is to win well-paying union jobs for all workers in semiconductor factories, to protect local environments, and to keep workers, their families, and community members safe from toxic chemicals. This week’s guests include Rand Wilson, a CCU Organizer with more than 40 years of experience working with a number of national and local unions; Joe Turmes, a Boise, Idaho, based engineer, artist, and activist who has spent nearly 30 years in the semiconductor industry, currently at Micron; and Max (appearing pseudonymously to protect their identity), a fab tech based in Oregon currently working to unionize their workplace.

articles.title: What Makes Somebody a Marxist?
articles.author: Vivek Chibber
articles.content: Karl Marx famously declared that he was not a Marxist. But his theoretical work spawned many branches of research, political movements, and heated debate. Can we identify a set of unifying ideas that make up Marxism? On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism , Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek look at the foundations of Marx’s writing and explain how Marxism has both developed and degenerated over the past century. Confronting Capitalism with Vivek Chibber is produced by Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy and published by Jacobin. You can listen to the full episode here . Melissa Naschek In our podcast and in your academic work, you consistently put forward a Marxist perspective on politics, theory, and the economy, but sometimes you also criticize aspects of Marxism. In what sense do you consider yourself a Marxist? Vivek Chibber Marxism is a social theory about how the world works, and it’s the theory that’s been used and mobilized by the socialist movement. So, analytically, socialism and Marxism are different things. That it’s a theory that’s not just meant to put forward ideas in the abstract but to actually provide organizers with information that they can use. This may sound self-explanatory, but actually the majority of theory does not concern itself with this. Vivek Chibber No, and there’s no particular reward in academia for doing socially relevant work. So most academics and journalists are in this middle-class milieu, and their fundamental motivation is upward advancement, just like it is for somebody in an insurance company or real estate agency or something like that. What these two periods had in common, though, was that because they were periods of social upheaval, a lot of middle-class people were drawn outside their normal class culture toward the world, and were then — if they were lucky enough to be in political organizations or around political organizations like communist parties, trade unions, and socialist parties — also disciplined by the culture of those institutions to try to make their ideas relevant to the world. And that gave them the motivation to really interrogate those ideas, to really think hard about them. And there’s enough of them around each other that they could push each other, they could hold each other accountable. And finally, because there were so many Marxist thinkers, it became kind of mainstream. Most intellectuals and academics today stay away from Marxism for two reasons. One is that it doesn’t really help their careers, and the other is it’s embarrassing. You feel like you’re the freak, and unless you have real self-confidence, unless you have a community around you, or unless you are in an organization or something like that, it’s hard to be the freak in the room. So you slowly get assimilated, and it pays because there’s better academic career advancement if you’re not a Marxist. So those were the two periods in which you saw enormous flourishing of Marxist theory for all of these reasons. When the labor movements ebb, when the political institutions and trade unions and parties are dismantled, the academics are absorbed back into their world of upward advancement and general contempt toward working people, which is what most middle-class people have, right? So in the 1940s, the 1950s, and the 1960s, this is what you see. And then by the 1990s onward, the same thing again. By the 1990s, academic and intellectual institutions were different from what they were in the 1950s, in that they were no longer totally dominated by white men. Now you also have women, and now you also have people of color in these institutions, and they now start finding that they are not given all the goodies that the white men were getting, and they start developing a social theory and social analyses fundamentally geared toward their experience of discrimination, of glass ceilings, etc. And that then became the new radicalism. The new radicalism was one where the greatest sin is not exploitation. It’s not the way in which the poor are ground into dust. The greatest sin became discrimination, or cultural appropriation, or of not being treated with the same kind of respect that somebody else is in these middle-class settings. And anybody who tries to bring class into this environment, into this analysis, tries to redirect attention toward the people who can’t make basic ends meet and don’t have social insurance or basic employment. That is a threat to this version of radicalism, which is firmly pointed single-mindedly toward the travails of the professional classes whose upward mobility and ambitions are being frustrated. That becomes now the new radicalism. The irony of this turn away from class is not that it promoted race or gender above class. It’s that it identified race and gender with a certain class constituency within those communities. So it’s not that, for example, anti-racism should be denigrated in favor of class politics. It’s that identity politics turned race politics into the worldview of wealthy black and brown people, of the professional classes and the business classes within the black community, within Latino and Asian communities. Melissa Naschek And their specific class interests. Vivek Chibber Marxism was always anti-racist. Always. Marxism always fought against patriarchal gender relations. But it conceptualized and approached them in a way that foregrounded and promoted the interests of working-class people of color and working-class women. That means that it was a class perspective on social identities. What identity politics did was narrow down race and gender and sexuality to the way it was experienced by these upwardly mobile professionals in academia and the professional classes. And so it isn’t that it substituted race for class. It’s that it brought in a version of race that only elites are interested in. It brought in a version of gender politics that only professional women and wealthy women are interested in. And that means that in order to actually more effectively fight race and gender oppression, you have to take it up in a way that working class people experience them. And their discrimination is only one small component of what they experience. For oppressed populations, the fundamental struggle, whether you’re a woman or a person of color or some other group, is still going to be housing, health care, jobs, childcare, things like that, which, for the professional classes, have just never been issues because they have all of those things. And so they focus single-mindedly on impediments to more upward mobility rather than the ways in which your class situation actually makes your gender and race situation worse than it is for the upwardly mobile. That was not true in the 1950s and ’60s, because it couldn’t be, because they were so uniformly shut out of these social institutions. And this is why now radicalism is not only largely useless to working people, but working people despise the radicals, because the radicals spend most of their time heaping scorn on the unwashed masses and want to keep attention directly fixed on the travails of what we call the professional-mangerial class. This is the essence of identity politics. What makes it new today is that it has captured the space of radical analysis that socialists and Marxists used to inhabit. As long as this form of radicalism is what we see on the Left, the Left will continue to be marginal, useless, and largely despised. articles.title: The European Green Party Attacks Solidarity With Palestine
articles.author: Daniel Finn
articles.content: There has been a virulent backlash in the British media against the Green Party of England and Wales since delegates at the party conference voted for a motion that brands Zionism as a racist ideology and supports the formation of a single democratic state in Palestine. As we have come to expect when British pundits and politicians are discussing Israel, nobody has seen fit to ask any Palestinians what they think about Zionism and what it has meant for them in practice. While Palestinians who live in Britain are studiously ignored, the media extends its search for critical voices to the rest of Europe. The Guardian reported on a statement from the European Green Party (EGP) that criticized the motion — “we unequivocally distance ourselves from it” — and suggested that the English and Welsh Greens were now “facing international ostracism.” The speed and severity of the response from the EGP contrasts sharply with its deafening silence about the shameful track record of the German Greens, the flagship of the European Green movement ever since the 1980s. The EGP never spoke out against the German party, even though its leaders campaigned against a ceasefire in Gaza, supplied weapons to Israel’s war machine, and branded Palestinian schools and hospitals as legitimate targets. The Peace of the Grave The Green politician Annalena Baerbock was Germany’s foreign minister when Israel began its onslaught against the people of Gaza in October 2023, and she remained in that post until May 2025. Her party had already demonstrated its hostility to Palestinian rights in 2019 when it voted to support a Bundestag motion that compared the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement to Nazism. There was a big increase in German arms shipments to Israel during the final months of 2023. Between October 2023 and May 2025, when Baerbock ended her stint as foreign minster, her government had issued arms export licences for transfers to Israel worth more than €485 million. Baerbock also threw the full weight of Germany’s foreign policy apparatus behind Israel. The woman who spoke about a “feminist foreign policy” was vehemently opposed to a ceasefire in Gaza as the death toll rose vertiginously. Her arguments against a ceasefire in November 2023 were patently absurd: For a ceasefire, Israel and Hamas would have to agree to stop shooting at each other. That would mean Israel would no longer be able to defend itself amid the ongoing barrage of missiles. If Hamas had continued firing missiles at Israel, of course, that would not have been a ceasefire at all. What Baerbock really found objectionable was the idea that Israel might have to stop firing missiles at Gaza. The following month, the German Foreign Office opposed a resolution at the UN General Assembly that called for a ceasefire. It insisted that Israel was entitled to keep going until its opponents surrendered unconditionally: “Only when Hamas lays down its arms will Israel no longer be forced to defend itself.” Shortly afterward, Baerbock cosigned an article with the British foreign secretary, David Cameron, that sought to rationalize the opposition of their governments to a ceasefire: We do not believe that calling right now for a general and immediate ceasefire, hoping it somehow becomes permanent, is the way forward. It ignores why Israel is forced to defend itself: Hamas barbarically attacked Israel and still fires rockets to kill Israeli citizens every day. Hamas must lay down its arms. Let us imagine that we did press Israel to cease all military operations forthwith. Would Hamas stop firing rockets? Would it release the hostages? Would its murderous ideology change? An unsustainable ceasefire, quickly collapsing into further violence, would only make it harder to build the confidence needed for peace. Racist contempt for Palestinian lives supplied the necessary undergirding for such arguments. By the time Baerbock and Cameron put their names to this screed, Israel had killed nearly twenty thousand people in Gaza. They shed crocodile tears for the victims — “too many civilians have been killed” — while studiously ignoring the evidence that mass slaughter was Israel’s intended goal, rooted in a “murderous ideology” that denies the right of Palestine to exist. The “peace” they had in mind for Gaza was the peace of the torture chamber and the mass grave. Simple Truths In January 2024, Baerbock immediately joined the Israeli campaign against the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), cutting off funding for the organization that supplied vital humanitarian aid to the people of Gaza. This move came just as Israel went on trial at the International Court of Justice, accused of violating the Genocide Convention. She later admitted that Israel had supplied no evidence to back up its allegations that UNRWA collaborated with Hamas. Over the course of the year, Baerbock modified her rhetoric in a way that mirrored the discursive games of the Biden administration, calling for a “humanitarian ceasefire” while her government continued to funnel arms to Israel. Israeli leaders had no reason to fear any consequences when they brushed aside such calls. In September 2024, she addressed the UN General Assembly in New York and explicitly legitimized Israeli attacks on civilian targets in Gaza: We have to face the dilemma that the values of the [UN] Charter can at times appear contradictory. Such as the inherent right to self-defence and the responsibility to protect civilians when civilians are misused as human shields. Resolving this is harder than simply exclaiming: “either — or,” “us against them.” Especially in this era of social media, where simple TikTok truths seem to blur out all complexity and nuance, sometimes even facts. We can see that with regard to the war in the Middle East. It is difficult to do justice to the brazen immorality of these remarks. By the time Baerbock spoke at the UN, there was already abundant evidence that Israel was systematically destroying the hospitals of Gaza. The World Health Organization documented 464 attacks on health care facilities between October 2023 and June 2024, resulting in 727 deaths and 933 injuries. For Baerbock to wave aside this evidence with an airy reference to “simple TikTok truths” suggested a capacity for shamelessness that is rare even in her chosen profession. Israel did not target Gaza hospitals because it believed that Hamas was using them as military bases. It targeted hospitals and the doctors who worked in them because they were giving people shelter and keeping them alive. This was part of a broader campaign against educational, cultural, and religious sites that was intended to make life impossible for the people of Gaza. Israeli leaders justified this carnage with robotic clichés about “human shields.” In case there was any doubt that Baerbock fully intended to endorse this alibi for mass murder, she bragged about it in a speech to the German parliament: We have made it clear time and again that self-defence means, of course, not only attacking terrorists, but also destroying them. This’s why I have made it so clear that when Hamas terrorists hide behind people, behind schools, then we end up in very difficult waters. But we’re not shying away from this. This is why I made it clear at the United Nations that civilian sites could lose their protected status if terrorists abuse this status. That’s what Germany stands for — and that’s what we mean when we refer to Israel’s security. Baerbock ignored a letter signed by three hundred academics that urged her to retract these comments on the grounds that they supplied “a flimsy justification for the genocidal campaign against Palestinian civilians.” After her departure from the German Foreign Office, she ascended to a new job as president of the UN General Assembly, where she sought to reinvent herself as a sassy, straight-talking champion of women’s rights: “As sports star Serena Williams once said: you call us crazy, we’ll show you what crazy can do.” Selective Indignation The EGP statement depicts the motion that the English and Welsh Green Party voted for last weekend as a fundamental departure from the agreed principles of the European Greens: “The resolution ‘Zionism is Racism’ as voted yesterday goes against our agreed positions of the EGP and its Member Parties, therefore as EGP we unequivocally distance ourselves from it.” It goes on to accuse Israel of genocide in the very next sentence: We condemn in the strongest terms the genocide against Palestinians and the human rights abuses committed by the current Israeli government and have consistently called for EU sanctions against Israel’s government. A diligent search of the EGP’s website will not reveal any statements distancing themselves from Baerbock’s conduct, unequivocally or otherwise. We can only conclude that branding Zionism as a racist ideology or calling for a “single democratic Palestinian state” based on “equal rights for all” is a greater sin in the eyes of the EGP than providing material support to what it correctly defines as a genocidal regime. The only sensible response from the English and Welsh Greens would be to roll their eyes in contempt. articles.title: Was Karl Kautsky Right About Ultra-Imperialism?
articles.author: Donald Parkinson
articles.content: Six weeks after the outbreak of World War I, as Europe’s great empires sent millions to their deaths, Karl Kautsky published an essay predicting something almost impossible to believe. In an article for Die Neue Zeit called “Der Imperialismus,” better known under the English title “Ultra-Imperialism,” Kautsky argued that the leading powers were, despite all evidence to the contrary, moving toward not endless conflict but peaceful cooperation. The claim quickly came to seem absurd. As the trenches filled with corpses and the war consumed an entire generation, Kautsky’s essay looked less like a penetrating analysis than a spectacular misreading of history. Today most young socialists encounter “Ultra-Imperialism” only as the foil for Vladimir Lenin’s Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism — a naive theory that mistook the realities of global capitalism and furnished an intellectual rationale for Kautsky’s increasingly centrist politics. But before tossing Kautsky’s “Ultra-Imperialism” into the dustbin of history, it’s worth looking at what he actually had to say. Kautsky’s theory begins with the premise that the smooth functioning of the capitalist economy relies on proportionality between sectors, in this case the agricultural and industrial sectors. The industrial sector, growing more quickly than the agrarian sector, creates a dual problem of underconsumption, where agricultural zones lack the purchasing power to buy from a growing pool of available industrial goods, as well as underproduction, where the agricultural sector is not productive enough to meet the demands of the growing industrial sector, leading to price spikes. The solution to this problem from the capitalist nations was imperialist expansion to secure new agrarian zones, leading to an era of free trade in which Britain was the indisputable “workshop of the world,” selling manufactured goods to a global countryside in exchange for raw materials and food. Yet it was obviously not in the interest of these nations to remain agrarian, and any country that could feasibly compete with Britain in manufacturing (the United States and Germany, for example) would reject free trade and embrace tariffs to invest in their own firms. As domestic industrial capacity grew, so did the need to find profitable investments overseas, leading industrial nations to export capital abroad to the global countryside of the agrarian zone. Yet the industrialized countries had no interest in seeing these poorer nations develop on their own terms and potentially become competitors themselves — hence the need for the industrialized nations to conquer, colonize, or otherwise dominate them. This need created conflict between the industrialized nations, which engaged in an arms race and armed conflict over the control of the global agrarian zones. It is here that Kautsky finds the root cause of the policy of imperialism. It is clear that for Kautsky, imperialism is a matter of policy, which he explicitly identifies with the arms race among capitalists in the rich industrialized countries. If the policy of free trade is to be associated with industrial capital, Kautsky associated imperialism with finance capital. Imperialism is a policy that is ultimately destabilizing for capitalism, as it not only intensifies resistance in the colonial and semicolonial world but also produces financial burdens on the proletariat in the industrialized countries. According to Kautsky, while there is an economic necessity for the continued subjugation of the agrarian zone by the rich countries — a subjugation that can only end with socialism — there is no economic necessity under capitalism for the imperialist arms race. In fact, the imperialist arms race was, in many ways, destabilizing for capitalism, a break with its inherent economic rationality. Hence, per Kautsky, “every far-sighted capitalist today must call on his fellows: capitalists of all countries, unite!” Rather than fratricidal violence, the future of capitalism was a cartel of the rich nations united as a “holy alliance of the imperialists.” Kautsky predicted that they’d be so exhausted by the massive social dislocation produced by the coming war that they would prefer self-preservation over further self-destruction. Capitalists, for Kautsky, were ultimately governed by their own ironclad rationality; peace was simply the rational play. Sure, this holy alliance of capitalists would still exploit and dominate the poor nations of the world as a global countryside, and Kautsky was clear that ultra-imperialism should be struggled against with as much vigor as was the more primitive phase of imperialism preceding it. But the perils of ultra-imperialism “lie in another direction, not in that of the arms race and the threat to world peace.” The exact nature of these perils is left unclear. One can easily see why Lenin and fellow revolutionaries found fault with the political logic at play here. For one, Kautsky seems to suggest that there is an enlightened bourgeoisie that can be appealed to, at least temporarily, as a means of negotiating a more sane and rational imperialism. At the very least, it seemed to promise a more peaceful form of capitalism down the line, despite the perilous road ahead. For Lenin, any period of peace and unity between capitalist powers could only be a temporary truce between periods of violent redivision of the world. If World War I made Kautsky’s thesis seem implausible, World War II, in which industrialized capitalist powers duked it out once again with even more terrifying weaponry, seemed to put it into further disrepute. Writing under the pseudonym E. Germain in 1955, Ernest Mandel bashed Kautsky’s theory of ultra-imperialism as being based on a “blindness to the contradictory, dialectical character of capitalist evolution, to the concentration of capital.” Concentration did not abolish competition so much as raise it to a higher level: as capital merged into national blocs, rivalry passed from firms fighting for markets to states fighting for territory. Yet as the years passed, the world increasingly came to resemble Kautsky’s vision of ultra-imperialism. The major capitalist powers did, in fact, form a holy alliance: the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The growing stature of the Soviet Union as a geopolitical force imposed a collective discipline on those powers’ ruling classes, uniting them under the leadership of the now global hegemon, the United States of America. A bipolar world quickly took shape while the global countryside emerged as a potentially independent force through a wave of decolonial revolutions. As newly independent states pursued their own paths of national development, they found themselves confronting a global system of multinational corporations and Bretton Woods institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. Together, these institutions constituted an internationally integrated system of finance capital that worked collectively to keep the world’s poorer nations in a position of dependency. For example, while Kwame Nkrumah’s 1965 Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism may carry a title that echoes Lenin’s famous tract, the world he describes seems closer to the ultra-imperialism described by Kautsky. Nkrumah portrays American and European corporations, banks, and states as operating through interlocking networks that cooperate to exploit Africa’s labor and natural resources. Institutions like Deutsche Bank and the Banque de Paris no longer appeared as antagonists locked in a scramble for colonies but as partners in the shared exploitation of the newly independent nations of the Third World. Had history, despite Lenin’s confidence, ended up vindicating Kautsky after all? Had the imperialist powers ultimately united into a single bloc to plunder the developing world? After the fall of the USSR, alternative socialist paths of development were practically foreclosed, with the United States emerging as the hegemon of a unipolar world. For some on the Left, like Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri in their work Empire , global capitalism had reached a new stage beyond imperialism, where the nation-state no longer had relevance and no country could claim to be an exploiting “core” in relation to an oppressed global “periphery.” Commentators would compare Hardt and Negri’s theory to Kautsky’s ultra-imperialism, but such comparisons misunderstand the latter’s theory, which never claimed that the division of the world between rich and poor countries would be overcome. Yet we should not be too quick to claim Kautsky’s theory of ultra-imperialism as vindicated. Growing tensions between the United States and its European allies, together with China’s emergence as a potential peer competitor to American hegemony, suggest that ultra-imperialism might have just been a temporary phase. The limits the United States has encountered in projecting power in places like the Persian Gulf and Ukraine indicate that we may be returning to an era of arms races and interimperialist rivalry. Perhaps Lenin was right after all: periods of cooperation among the capitalist powers are merely interludes before the next round of great-power conflict. Time will tell. As of now, we can only be certain that capitalism inherently produces rapacious inequality among the nations, and that socialism alone can properly address it. articles.title: As Trump’s Coalition Breaks, Can the Left Pick Up the Pieces?
articles.author: Conor Lynch
articles.content: The coalition that sent Donald Trump back to the White House in 2024 marked the culmination of a long-term political realignment that conservative authors and activists had anticipated since the 1970s. Fifty years earlier, right-wing commentators like William Rusher, then the publisher of National Review , were busy sketching a blueprint for the new majority that they hoped would finally bring them to power after decades of Democratic rule. That majority, according to Rusher and other “New Right” thinkers, would be built around the same working class that had long served as a pillar of the New Deal coalition. In his own words, the Right would construct a “Great Coalition” made up of the “producers of America,” in which he naturally included “businessmen, workers and farmers.” These “producers” would be united in their hostility toward a “rapacious new non-producing class” of “liberal verbalists” and their “huge welfare constituency” — that is, liberal members of the professional middle class and the poor. Back then, Democrats were still widely considered the party of the working class and Republicans the party of the affluent and college educated. By 2024, these voting blocs had largely flipped. While Kamala Harris captured an impressive 56 percent of voters with a college degree, she lost those without any college education by 13 points. Just twelve years earlier, Barack Obama had narrowly carried noncollege voters by 3 points, while Mitt Romney had won college-educated voters by four. The same trends were apparent for income: Harris won a majority of voters who earned over $100,000, while her Republican opponent won 52 percent of those making between $30,000 and $100,000 (once again the opposite of 2012, when Romney won 54 percent of upper-income voters). These results led to many predictable claims that the 2024 election would finally usher in a new era of Republican domination thanks to the party’s newfound support from the working class. Yet even at the height of the Right’s post-2024 triumphalism, one basic fact undercut the story of the GOP’s working-class transformation. While Trump had indeed won more working-class voters than any other Republican in the modern era, he was also the runaway favorite of business elites and the billionaire class. According to one analysis , the top three hundred billionaire donors in 2024 donated to Republican candidates by a remarkable five-to-one margin. The fervent support Trump received from some of the wealthiest men on the planet was difficult to reconcile with the GOP’s supposed transformation into a humble party of the working man and woman. Even though economic issues like inflation and affordability shaped the 2024 election, the Trump coalition was held together more by cultural grievances than by any kind of shared economic outlook. When right-wing populists railed against “elites,” they were almost always talking about cultural and political elites rather than economic ones. In fact, it was sometimes wealthy oligarchs who denounced these “elites” the loudest. This pattern was apparent throughout the Biden years, when a growing number of right-wing billionaires cast themselves as populist crusaders taking on a powerful cabal of “woke” elites. When Elon Musk staged his hostile takeover of Twitter and immediately fired the majority of its staff (the “laptop class,” he called them), the billionaire was hailed by the Right as a populist hero. Though Musk was following the old playbook of corporate raiders, one commentator celebrated it as a “revolt by entrepreneurial capital against the professional-managerial class regime that otherwise everywhere dominates.” This portrait of the richest man in the world as an embattled underdog taking on a powerful class of parasitic elites aligned perfectly with the Right’s vision of America’s class divide. According to that distorted vision, it’s not ultrawealthy oligarchs but college-educated professionals and middle managers who make up the country’s true ruling class , leeching off the heroic efforts of industrialists and entrepreneurs at the top and blue-collar workers at the bottom. Another anti-woke crusader, Vivek Ramaswamy (who’s also a billionaire ), echoed this narrative during his 2024 presidential campaign, declaring that the real class divide is between the “managerial class and the everyday citizen.” This was a convenient line for oligarchs, as it all but erased economics from class. In a world where the true elites were college-educated professionals and underpaid bureaucrats in the “deep state,” plutocrats could sell themselves as counterelites taking on the all-powerful ruling class. They could also bill themselves as natural allies of the working class, united in their shared dislike of hypereducated managerial elites and their “woke” ideology (never distinguishing, of course, between basic social justice concerns and more rancorous variants of identity politics). The big question after the 2024 election was whether the Trump coalition could survive once billionaire priorities and working-class interests inevitably clashed. Not even two years later, the answer has become increasingly apparent. The cracks that appeared in the Trump coalition early in his second term have since widened into deep fractures. Working-class voters, in particular, are rapidly turning away from the president and the GOP. According to a June review of polling by the New York Times , Trump’s standing with white voters without college degrees has cratered since the start of his second term, especially compared with the same point in his first term. In 2018, these voters approved of Trump’s handling of the economy by 30-point margins ahead of that year’s midterms; today they disapprove in some polls by equally large margins. Research by Jared Abbott and Joan C. Williams has confirmed the growing fissures in the Trump coalition. The overall number of “Trump waverers” has increased since the start of this year, according to their polling, with about a quarter of Trump voters now saying they are unlikely to vote Republican in 2028. Lower-income Trump voters are by far the most likely to say they won’t vote for a Republican in two years, with nearly a third of those earning under $50,000 wavering, compared with 18 percent of those earning above $100,000. (Unsurprisingly, working-class voters of color have pulled away the most.) Trump and Republicans are bleeding working-class support for obvious reasons. The cost-of-living crisis has progressively worsened over the past two years thanks to Trump’s own harebrained policies , while the GOP’s signature legislative achievement is widely (and accurately) perceived by voters as helping the wealthy rather than the working class. Trump’s overt corruption and clear favoritism toward the billionaire wing of his coalition have further alienated many working-class Americans. The Right’s Misfortune, the Left’s Opportunity The breakdown of the Trump coalition bodes well for Democrats this November, but it hardly guarantees that working-class voters will swing back to the left. What is increasingly certain is that a winning left-wing coalition will have to unite noncollege voters — to use a functional if imperfect class proxy — with the college graduates who now make up one of the most reliable voting blocs for Democrats and the socialist movement . The good news is that voters across the so-called diploma divide have been converging on economic views, even as many real social and cultural differences remain. Recent polling and new research consistently show that economic populism is the antidote to right-wing populism, which largely succeeds by replacing economic conflict with cultural division. Right-wing populism’s one move, observes Joan Williams in her recent book Outclassed: How the Left Lost the Working Class and How to Win Them Back , is to “take economic anger and direct it away from the Merchant Right, toward people of color and the Brahmin Left.” To counter this playbook, Williams argues that the Left must “redirect the anger toward economic elites, acknowledge the failings of political elites, and learn how to avoid making themselves the target of anger against cultural elites.” Williams uses the terminology of French economist Thomas Piketty, who famously distinguished between the Merchant Right and Brahmin Left to explain the political realignments across most Western democracies over the last half century. During the postwar decades, liberal democracies were largely bifurcated along class lines, with the working class supporting center-left parties and affluent and college-educated voters leaning right. As we’ve seen, that order fractured in the late twentieth century and evolved into today’s system of “multiple elites,” with business elites moving further to the right and college-educated professionals veering left. Under this new order, elites fought primarily over “post-material” concerns. As Piketty wrote in 2020, both sides were “strongly attached to the existing economic system” because it served the “interests of both intellectual elites and economic and financial elites.” Today that neoliberal consensus has begun to unravel, in large part because of growing skepticism among college-educated voters toward the winner-take-all economy their predecessors once favored. According to an analysis of the 2024 election and preelection surveys by the Center for American Progress, college-educated voters are now about as likely as working-class voters (defined as those without a college degree) to back progressive economic policies like taxing the rich, supporting unions, and raising the federal minimum wage. This partly explains the recent electoral success of left-wing populists like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, who have been elevated by younger college graduates who now broadly reject the neoliberal politics of the past forty years. Many of these voters fall into what reporter Noam Scheiber calls the “college-educated working class” in his recent book , Mutiny , which documents the organizing efforts of college graduates working in historically unorganized and underpaid sectors. “Young, downwardly mobile college grads [appear] to be embracing more radical politics as they [feel] put-upon at work or marginalized in the job market,” notes Scheiber. These trends are more pronounced among younger graduates and those working in the more precarious and low-paying professions, such as education, social work, and journalism. Yet even some members of the historically more stable and affluent professions appear to be moving away from their traditional conservatism as they confront new economic realities and professional pressures. In the past, college graduates were generally more optimistic about their economic prospects than those without degrees, but today polling shows the reverse. “For the first time in the past three years, college-educated workers are the most pessimistic about the job market, and younger workers are more likely than older ones to say it is a bad time to find a good quality job,” wrote pollsters at Gallup in March. The discontent that has spread throughout much of the white-collar workforce has long been familiar to members of the working class. After decades of neoliberal policies that have undermined workers’ rights and standards of living, employment has now grown more precarious for college graduates and white-collar employees as well. At the same time, wealth has grown ever more concentrated at the very top. These trends have only accelerated in the second Trump era: while America’s billionaires saw their wealth soar by more than 30 percent over the past year, labor’s share of business output fell to its lowest level on record at the end of 2025. In her 1989 book on the professional middle class, Fear of Falling , Barbara Ehrenreich described the “defining dream of the American left” as one in which “discontented members of the [professional] middle class might join the working-class majority in a political effort to redistribute both power and wealth downward.” Two years after a very different kind of coalition sent Trump back to the White House, the question now facing the Left is whether a more durable populist coalition can be built from its ruins. articles.title: “The Spanish People Will Remember Who Betrayed Them”
articles.author: Pablo Bustinduy
articles.content: Could it be that Spain hasn’t let you know? None of you — none of you — is the person who has two weeks to find an apartment without knowing where they’ll go. And none of you is the person living in fear of an eviction notice arriving. None of you is the person counting the months until their lease ends, waiting for their landlord to say something. None of you is the person coming home from work today with the radio on to hear the result of this vote. None of you is one of those people, yet you are going to decide for them. You are going to decide what happens with their lives. Congressman [Gabriel] Rufián said earlier, and I agree, “Whoever comes up here today to argue against these two decree-laws should publicly reveal whom they have met with and who has called them in recent weeks.” I know whom many of the congresspeople voting on these decrees today have met with and who has called them. They have met with a woman who has lived for forty-five years in the La Latina neighborhood, near here, in the very apartment where her husband and mother passed away, who is now awaiting an eviction notice because another one of these scoundrels has inherited the whole building and filled it with illegal tourist apartments, all with the collusion of the Madrid City Council. I know there are congresspeople who have met with the seventy-five tenant families in the Casa de Alba, also threatened with eviction in order to turn their lifelong homes into vacation rentals, rooms for foreigners, and, yes, more illegal tourist apartments, and who, thanks to the lease extensions that the Partido Popular, Vox, and Junts voted against six months ago, could renegotiate their contracts and remain in their homes. We have met with these people. I know there are congresspeople who have met with families living in fourteen buildings that belonged to the archbishopric of Madrid and were sold to a vulture fund, which in turn sold them to another vulture fund, which then sold them to yet another vulture fund — all three of them foreign — and who are living in buildings without lights in the hallways and at risk of collapse, because they want to throw everyone out in order to convert them into luxury housing for purchase by the foreign oligarchy to whom you people are selling off this country. Today is not about parliamentary arithmetic. It is not about negotiations between political groups, not about amendments, not about the interpretation of this or that article. Today is about a class conflict. Today is about defending an international oligarchy that is extracting rents from the hard-fought wages of this country’s working classes to divvy them among themselves as dividends without even paying taxes on it in Spain. To vote no on these decrees today is to defend the interests of that oligarchy and turn your back on your people. You can shout Spain’s or Catalonia’s name at the top of your lungs. To vote against these decrees today is to betray your people to serve the sole cause and banner of rentism. And I tell you this: you do not realize the magnitude of what you are doing. Often there is a vast gap between the debates held inside this chamber and what the people out there want. Rarely has that chasm been as astronomical as what is happening here today in this session, in this chamber. Very rarely. And if this is happening, if you are here today and must put your names to this disgrace, the disgrace of leaving millions of Spaniards unprotected, it is because the people have risen up, because a public outcry sweeps through the streets of this country, declaring that you do not represent them, that you offer no solutions to their problems. And today once again they will insist on it. And if the people of this country have achieved that, they have achieved something even more valuable: demonstrating an incontrovertible truth to the citizenry as a whole. That truth is that all the rights of working people have been won through struggle, that none were conceded and none were gifted, and that all were wrested from the oligarchy by organizing, mobilizing, and protesting. And perhaps today you will again strike down measures designed to protect the working people of this country. You may succeed in this today, but I tell you with the utmost solemnity, the right to housing in this country will prevail above the interests of the rentier class you represent. In this country, 20 percent of the population rents. Some 5 percent of households receive income from rent. You speak of small landlords, but over the last fourteen years the number of Spanish families that own a property has fallen by 14 percent. Large owners have quadrupled their real estate assets during this period. Today 61 percent of rentals in Spain are owned by multi-property landlords and corporate entities. Six out of ten. In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, that figure is far higher. To the members of the Junts: in the city of Barcelona, sixteen thousand people own two hundred thousand rentals. The income of these multi-property owners is, on average, four times that of a tenant family. The net worth of these multi-property landlords is 450 times that of the tenants. The rental market in this country functions as a mechanism for the transfer of incomes from the working classes, who have the least, to the propertied classes, who have the most. The measures outlined in today’s decree-laws entail a reverse transfer: €624 million passed from landlords to tenants. So this is not about parliamentary arithmetic. What you are going to vote down today is precisely what would prevent €624 million from going into the pockets of those who have already quadrupled the rent on working families, paid out of workers’ pockets with the fruits of their labor. That is what you are voting for. And there will be no flag-waving. There will be no outbursts, no obscene theatrics. You’ll have the keys to your own homes when [Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez] Feijóo governs. The only keys we’ve seen are those to [Popular Party politician Isabel Díaz] Ayuso’s penthouse. Seven million euros in public funds. That is the Popular Party’s housing policy. Voting to evict people from their homes; voting to let them raise the rent by 40 percent. So they throw you out on the street. To leave you wondering if you’ll have to change your children’s schools because you can no longer afford the rent where you’ve lived your whole life, in the neighborhood where your parents and grandparents lived, forcing you out so an illegal tourist rental can take its place (while [Mayor of Madrid José Luis Martínez-] Almeida looks the other way) or so a foreign oligarch can have his little apartment in Madrid. You do not defend the Spanish people. You defend the rich. You have neither a flag nor any shame. And it isn’t just about the numbers. In this country, millions upon millions of people have had common experiences, which have now been brought out into the open and acknowledged. The management company that you ask to paint the walls, since they haven’t in twenty-five years, and they just pass you a can of paint. The landlord who tells you the rent is going up 40 percent because your lease is expiring but tells you to think it over, because a home is, after all, what’s most important in life. The corporation that keeps your security deposit, making up some excuse, or forces you to pay signing fees, despite these being lies — and illegal — or that charges you to view an apartment, or invents some nonpayment insurance or management fees that you have to pay because, “Hey, if you don’t, someone else will.” Just imagine what people out there are going to think about how you vote today. While you are here not making a scene, not beating your chests but making political calculations of how you’ll fare in the elections or what’s most convenient, people outside are following closely because they have to renew their contract and haven’t heard a word yet, or have suddenly been told the rent is going up 60 percent because “that’s the market, buddy.” Imagine what people are going to think when you vote no, when the only thing they can afford is a room in an apartment where a whole family used to live, but it was purchased by a vulture fund that put up partitions to cram six or seven families in because, hey, that’s the market, buddy. Just imagine what people will think when you vote no, while week after week they receive notices about an impending eviction or calls for people to help stop one. Imagine what they will think as they watch their blocks and their neighborhoods fill up with illegal tourist rentals, with the wretched sounds of their luggage, watch how their local shops close down and how the place they called home, their neighborhood, where they wanted to raise their children, was turned into a theme park for those who can afford it, leaving the rest to fend for themselves. Just imagine what working-class people will think of their political representatives. And when I say you fail to grasp this, I mean you think this won’t affect you. Members of the Popular Party: among your voters, there are two times as many tenants as landlords. Members of Vox: among your voters, there are three times as many tenants as landlords. The same applies to you, members of Junts. What do you think? That right-wing people aren’t worried when their leases expire? That they aren’t worried about having to move to a different neighborhood? That they aren’t worried? Mr Quero [Carlos Hernández, member of Congress for Vox], you were just speaking about those young people who have been apartment-hunting for months. I hope it isn’t your sister, Mr Quero. I hope she isn’t looking for an apartment. Because when we brought the measure to extend rental contracts here, you told me, “My sister is in that situation. She could benefit from it; it would really help her. But I’m going to vote no because, well, between BlackRock and my sister, I choose BlackRock.” That is the difference between you and me, Mr Quero. I don’t know how your sister votes or what her ideology is, but I prioritize defending her interests and rights over those of the big multinationals. And you don’t. You don’t. You are selling out your country. I ask that the people who are outside not be misled; it is the big multinationals, the financiers, the real estate lobby, that are funding a fearmongering campaign to poison the discourse and deceive you. What is being voted on today is actually quite simple. There are five million Spanish citizens — of all ideological leanings, who vote for all the parties, and who live in every region — whose leases are expiring. What is being voted on today is an extension of those contracts for two years, without any rent increases. They are going to vote no on that. What is being voted on today is freezing remaining rental contracts at a 0 percent increase, because working-class people in Spain already spend enough of their incomes on rent. What is being voted on today is putting an end to the obscene, obscene fraud of seasonal rentals and contracts for rooms that they can lock you in each year, raising your rent, saying, “No, no — look, next year it’s going to be €300 more. Why? Because I say so. And if you’re not able to figure it out, this is over.” Today we have the chance to vote yes and put an end to the fraud surrounding room rentals, which affects the most vulnerable people in this country. Yet you are going to vote no. You have been told about anti-eviction protections many times, but it makes no difference. The thing is, we don’t even need to say it. Every eviction that takes place after this vote will bear the names of those who vote no on these decrees today — whether they are from the PP, Vox, or Junts. It will bear their names. And yes, I have the honor of defending the decree-law on rent stabilization today. This is the primary demand of the popular movement that has flooded the streets and shaped this country’s political agenda, finally bringing the number one issue facing working people in this country to the table in this parliament. Yes, the automatic renewal of rental contracts. And what a week you’ve all had, right? Good grief — communism , interventionism — just look at the lengths we’re supposedly willing to go in order to attack small property owners. This is the model that exists in England, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, and across much of Europe, based on a principle that is quite simple to grasp: the need of the citizen — whether an individual, a family, or a worker — for housing does not simply expire every five years. And so, when a contract ends, the prevailing notion is, “Well, the contract is over,” effectively throwing you back to the law of the jungle. “That’s the market for you, my friend; prices are up 40 percent, and if you can’t figure it out, well, too bad.” This model, however, establishes that when a contract expires, it renews automatically unless there is a valid reason not to renew it. And people cried foul, shouting interventionism and claiming the market would collapse. This sounds familiar, doesn’t it, Madam Vice President? Raising the minimum wage was supposed to destroy the Spanish economy. Strengthening workers’ rights? Good heavens! What would become of Spain’s productive fabric? Labor reform — providing stability, making jobs permanent — was deemed outrageous. It was supposed to sink the Spanish economy. Yet here we are with the highest employment levels in our history and growing at a pace that none of the countries advocating those other measures are able to reach. Well, of course granting rights to working people makes things better. And they say, “It’s outrageous, simply outrageous, that if a landlord wants to kick a family out onto the street without justification, they have to pay compensation!” Just imagine if these people were the ones drafting labor laws today. They’d say exactly the same thing. What a scandal — an employer having to compensate a worker for firing them without cause? Imagine if these people were the ones building a public education, health care, or pension system today. Yet they say it openly: “The country’s retirees are the biggest economic threat we face.” They voted against adjusting pensions. Why? Because the retirees are the enemy. But blaming migrants, blaming retirees, blaming the Left, blaming whoever is convenient — it’s all a way to distract from what they’re actually doing: constantly shielding the interests of the oligarchy, serving the elite, and betraying the working class. That’s simply what they always do. They’re parasites, aren’t they? Living off handouts. A family receiving €525 from social security is “living off handouts.” A retiree who has a pension after a lifetime of work is a “threat to public finances.” Yet someone who inherited seven apartments and lives off them without ever lifting a finger? That’s an entrepreneur. That’s the person we defend. What hypocrisy and what a betrayal of the people. I truly believe that today you are going to make a political mistake that you will regret for a long time. You may be convinced that you can manage the media, stick to your schedules, and serve your own partisan interests. But in politics and democracy, there is something far greater — far greater, more important, and more powerful — than lobbies, private agendas, and all the money held by those who reap dividends and profits at the expense of the working class. That force is the social power of a conscious, awakened people who are out there right now demanding of their representatives and the authorities that they stop this shameful practice of looking the other way, blaming the opposition, and claiming that the situation is simply too complex. Today there are solutions on the table — minimal solutions, to be sure. They represent a first step toward balancing the scales, making life a little easier for the working class, and bringing stability and certainty to their lives. I can assure you that the people are going to remember. They will remember those who betrayed them.
