articles.title: The Detroit Socialist is Not Dirty Laundry
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: By Chris W. Miehle printing press in operation, with freshly printed copy on the cylinder. Photo credit: Douglas W. Jones via Wikimedia Commons At the 8/7 Steering Committee meeting, a new set of guidelines for our Detroit Socialist newspaper was brought forward, including number five on internal debates: 5. We should strive to keep internal debates and disagreements internal . We should not make it a habit to air our proverbial dirty laundry. At the end of the day, we are all comrades and we all want to achieve socialism. There is no reason to give our enemies ammunition to use against us. Internal debates are important and are critical to the democratic process, which is why they are better suited to our chapter’s internal discussion platforms and processes. This guideline was met with pushback from Steering Committee members Jon Mukes and Mohamd Z., as well as other chapter members in attendance. Comrade Mo suggested that such a contentious issue should be referred to a General Membership meeting, but that proposal was not taken up and it was sent back to the Newspaper Committee while the rest of the guidelines were passed. At the newspaper Zoom meeting on 8/13, it was proposed that articles labeled “internal debates” would be placed in the chapter Discord, rather than in the Detroit Socialist, so that they are not available for public consumption. Any debate article could be published in the Detroit Socialist only with a hidden link not visible on the site, or it would have to be published with an accompanying counterpoint article as part of the same post. After yet more pushback from Mohamd Z., myself and others, around what constituted an “internal debate,” an extra newspaper meeting was scheduled for 8/20. That meeting was attended by nearly every Metro Detroit member of the Groundwork caucus, as well as members of Bread and Roses, Marxist Unity Group, the Detroit Democracy Coalition, and independent members. Newspaper meetings average about five attendees, including the editors. The Groundwork members favored the guidelines; the Bread and Roses, Marxist Unity Group, and Detroit Democracy Coalition members opposed them. At the August 30th Steering Committee meeting, the committee voted to adopt the updated internal debate guideline. It’s difficult to parse the actual guideline from the agitation for the guideline (full text here ), but the most relevant portion is this: For the purposes of this proposal, internal debate and discussion will be defined as follows: “Discussion that directly affects a strategic decision taken by the membership imminently.”… Should a member still wish to publish their work on an internal debate in The Detroit Socialist , they will have the option to either publish it on an unlisted link on The Detroit Socialist ’s Medium page — meaning that only individuals with the link may access the work — or, members may publish in The Detroit Socialist , but it will be published on the same page of an article with an opposing view. These guidelines would turn The Detroit Socialist into nothing more than a promotional brochure — a place to “celebrate our victories” but not to tackle any difficult political discussions. Taking political debate out of The Detroit Socialist , or trying to hide it away in a Detroit-only Discord server, will prevent uncaucused comrades from influencing national DSA politics, cut off our chapter from the national DSA movement, rob this chapter of its best forum for political discussion, and debilitate the political development of our membership and the wider working class. The Detroit Socialist is the only place for uncaucused comrades in our chapter to set out their own political positions for a broader public audience. Whereas caucused members of our chapter (a very small minority) will be able to publish under their caucus letterhead, those without a caucus who want to publish something on internal Detroit politics will be relegated to a quiet cul-de-sac where no one in the broader organization, or the wider working class, will be able to read it. This will force chapter members to join a caucus if they want to have a voice in the wider national discourse and create a built-in privilege for chapter members who are already part of a caucus. There is no “local issue” when DSA is involved. Many other chapters are likely engaging in similar debates as Metro Detroit, or they likely soon will be. Issues like: the adoption of email voting, how to rewrite bylaws, whether or not to endorse a candidate with only a tenuous connection to the chapter. It is important that every member of our chapter has an opportunity to write and be published in a paper that can be shared nationally, because as DSA members we are part of a national party, and as socialists we are part of a global movement. Decisions taken by Metro Detroit DSA will change the local and national political situation, influence the way DSA is perceived as a whole, and hopefully provide a guide for how other chapters can organize in their area. Internal debate in The Detroit Socialist is a vital stream of information for other chapters to understand the political conditions within our chapter and we have an obligation to openly share this discourse with them. Transformation of the working class from political objects to political subjects is one of the most important tasks of DSA as the nascent party of the working class. We need to show people that when they are collectively organized, they can enact their will on the world. This political development requires that workers can articulate for themselves what our party is fighting for. The Detroit Socialist is a training ground for members of the working class to build themselves into political thinkers who can construct nuanced arguments in long-form articles. The current political and cultural situation shows a dire need for long-form writing to be defended as a necessary skill for human flourishing. With AI slop becoming a blight on everyday life, it’s our socialist duty to defend and develop the human ability to think for oneself ( The Detroit Socialist expressly forbids AI-written articles). Writing is a unique and edifying form of thought, and by writing I mean setting down one’s thoughts in a long piece, not slapping a quip in a discord chat. There’s a reason Elon Musk spends all his time posting on Twitter: he’s a moron. And we will be condemning our chapter to moronhood if all we have for internal discourse is a Slack or Discord forum that’s essentially constructed the same way as a Facebook comment section. We already had an online forum for political discussion: the Slack channel, which many members already avoid because the level of discourse was usually low, poorly constructed, and at times devolved into ad hominems. This is not necessarily the fault of the participants. The medium is simply unsuited for intellectually rigorous debate. The Discord will likely experience all of the same problems. I challenge anyone to say they gained more intellectually from reading a 100+ reply Slack thread than from reading an article. I can say as the Political Education Co-chair, we do not ask people to read forum posts before attending New Member Political Education; we ask them to read articles. The writing in The Detroit Socialist comes from the same intellectual tradition as the pieces we do read as part of the curriculum. Marx, Lenin, Luxembourg– take your pick. They developed their thinking and the politics of the working class as a whole by debating political points in publications that were freely available to the masses. These were not writings that were hidden away for only party members to be able to view (as long as they weren’t censored by the state); they were shared and discussed by members of the working class who were not necessarily formal members of a socialist party. These writings are still read and discussed today. The great socialist theorists never feared airing their “dirty laundry,” because there’s nothing dirty about disagreement in a democratic organization. We should be proud of a robust culture of political debate and of our transparency as an organization. A pair of articles debating a political point are not a pair of dirty socks, they are red banners. It is not shameful that we debate, it is our socialist honor. There is concern that allowing certain points of view to be expressed in The Detroit Socialist will make our chapter look bad. For example, when Anthony D. argued against endorsing Donavan McKinney , it was said of the article, “It was bad for Donavan and it was bad for us.” The article was shared by a Metro Phoenix DSA page. Critics argued that this article confused readers and made it seem as if the chapter opposed Donovan’s endorsement. I think that confusion was cleared up when we voted to endorse him. But, if that doesn’t assuage these concerns, perhaps The Detroit Socialist can do what literally every other newspaper does and put a big “OPINION” above articles that aren’t meant to reflect the views of the chapter. If there is still concern over disagreements in this chapter making Metro-Detroit DSA look bad, I encourage the supporters of these restrictive guidelines to address disagreement the democratic way: make your case to membership and win your comrades over to your point-of-view through well-reasoned arguments. Maybe write an article in The Detroit Socialist ? Chris W. is a law student and an uncaucused member of the Democracy Coalition. The Detroit Socialist is Not Dirty Laundry was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: No, Digger Is Not a Misunderstood Masterpiece
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: You may have heard already that Digger , the new film cowritten and directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu ( The Revenant, Birdman ) and starring Tom Cruise, is an expensive box-office bomb that got many annihilating reviews . One of the better ones sums it up perfectly: “It’s like being trapped inside a tuba for two hours.” Bad news travels fast. And I’m going to further speed it along by providing an all-spoiler review, so consider yourself warned. This is in order to convince you that you’d be better off staying home watching Dr. Strangelove , Stanley Kubrick’s scathingly funny and incisive 1964 protest against world-ending insanity, which set the template for satirical black comedy for generations to come. Cue the predictable guardians of art and high culture emerging to defend Digger from us lowbrow proles who can’t appreciate cinematic brilliance and originality when they see it. See bits of it in previews, that is. They’re not crazy enough to actually go see the whole gruelingly unfunny and uninvolving movie. Very few people are, besides all the embittered film critics obligated to see Digger , sitting there alone in vast dark theaters trying to come up with new adjectives to describe their own jaded disaffection. As happens much more frequently than is generally acknowledged when it comes to films, the lowbrow proles are right. Digger is dead on arrival. All that big-budget prestige-picture money, all that great acting talent (John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons), all that lushly beautiful cinematography (Emmanuel Lubezki) and production design (Dennis Gassner and Richard L. Johnson), all that topical relevance, and for what? So you can watch Tom Cruise, nearly unrecognizable in gray hair, old-age makeup and prosthetics, and a fake potbelly, stomping around braying his lines as the title character Digger Rockwell, a crazily overconfident Texas oil tycoon tasked with preventing the ultimate world-destroying climate catastrophe that his own massive oil-drilling company created. The Big Meta “Twist” Falls Flat Signing big star Tom Cruise presumably got Iñárritu that extravagant reported budget of $125 million to make what amounts to a ponderous art film. You know the kind of art film I mean, the one that reveals partway through that all the characters shouting and crying and vomiting and making faces all over the place are in fact actors performing roles in a play — which is the big twist in Digger . At a certain point, Tom Cruise even stops hollering in an overripe, hog-calling Texas accent and speaks in his own voice in order to complain to the play’s director that he finds the Digger character “cartoonish” and feels “disconnected” from him and the whole experience. If this film weren’t so enervating, that would be the moment to yell at the screen, “You and me both, Tommy boy!” But no one’s got that kind of energy, not when the camera is heading backstage to show us that this is all actually a production of a theatrical cult hit called Fossil Fools . It seems the survivors of horrific climate catastrophes that occurred in the real world and wiped out much of the human population find it cathartic to watch those disasters replayed onstage, along with the downfall of Digger. It’s not that everyone involved in the production — the Digger production, I mean, not the Fossil Fools production — isn’t trying hard to sell the material. Part of the misery of watching it is seeing all the actors struggling to put their undeveloped characters across in wearying scenes full of rotten dialogue. Tom Cruise is generally effortful and a bit exhausting anyway — it’s part of his star persona — but as Digger he wears you out a quarter of the way into the film. Then there are the fabulous actors in supporting roles giving their all. John Goodman plays President Compson, another loud idiot, who’s grappling with the world-ending scenario created by Digger while suffering from “a-s cancer.” It’s a deadly affliction which will turn out to be convenient because he’ll be safely under the knife at Walter Reed Hospital when someone has to answer for the recent massive catastrophe. The subservient vice president, called “Eddie” throughout and played by Michael Stuhlbarg ( A Serious Man ), is deputized to face the enraged governing body. Meanwhile, Dr Nirav Ganesh (Riz Ahmed of Four Lions and Nightcrawler ), the earnest scientist who heads Digger’s environmental safety team, tries in vain to get any of the blowhards in charge to listen to him before it’s too late. An Astonishing Waste of Talent Other phenomenal actors are entirely wasted in nothing roles. Sandra Hüller, who came to international prominence in Anatomy of a Fall and The Zone of Interest , plays a few scenes as Emma, Digger’s much younger, cluelessly self-centered half-sister and business partner who’s allowed to run a company dedicated to clean energy that Digger treats as a joke. Jesse Plemons roams into scenes in the framing narrative about putting on the play, because he’s portraying Kenny Rockwell, Digger’s nephew, who owns the rights to the play Fossil Fools and encourages the cast to carry on mocking his ridiculous destroyer-of-worlds family because it’s cathartic for the play’s audiences. Burn Gorman, an excellent English character actor whom you’ll recognize if you’re a BritBox subscriber, literally has no lines and only one bit of business — an absurdly overdone patriotic salute when President Compson launches nuclear weapons at the massive ice shelf that broke off from Greenland and is about to crash into the western coast of the European continent, causing massive damage and loss of life. Nuking things, always the recommendation of military brass, only creates more problems, however. Featured in many more scenes and frankly performed with greater care is an animatronic white cat named Maggie, the only creature that Digger loves. She’s thirty years old and dying of several fatal conditions, a pitiable creature cruelly kept alive by the moronically doting Digger. That’s all played for laughs, by the way, just to give you a sense of Iñárritu’s comic stylings. It’s depressing to read about the ten-year development of this film involving writer-director Iñárritu and star-producer Tom Cruise. Iñárritu says the “spine” of the project was always Digger’s long monologue delivered to the European Parliament midway through the film, in which Digger admits to all charges against him about enriching himself through endless oil drilling and environmental despoliation, and covering up studies that would’ve provided proof for scientists trying to awaken the public to the dangers of fossil fuel reliance. Digger then proceeds to blame all the ordinary people in the world for this. He keeps the oil pumping because we all selfishly want to heat and cool our homes and drive cars and have cell phones. According to Iñárritu, he gave Digger ultimate persuasive power in this central scene because, as he puts it, “I’m not interested in pointing fingers or reducing the film to a political commentary or a right or left thing.” For Iñárritu, “we are all part of this madness.” It’s with a weary sense of inevitability that we watch this scene, which shifts blame to the struggling masses just trying to get by in a world run by vicious self-serving plutocrats. It doesn’t even make sense in terms of the rest of the film, which is dedicated to mocking the monstrous venality and cluelessness of billionaires and the politicians who serve them. Nevertheless, Iñárritu still wants to know if all of us relatively powerless people are now ready to dig deep and sacrifice any creature comforts we might have in order to save the world. For him, it’s all in our power to do it somehow. At the end of the film, the audiences shown flocking to see Fossil Fools to gloat over Digger’s demise are all wrong, failing to learn the proper lesson from the ongoing apocalypse — that “there are no good or bad people” and we all have to work together, kumbaya. This is a message that might have been convincing in the early 2010s. In 2026, with plenty of genuinely very bad people at the top of both our government and our economy — people who seem to even embrace their villainous powers — it falls very, very flat. articles.title: Lula Is in Danger of Losing Brazil’s Presidency
articles.author: Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
articles.content: The first round of Brazil’s elections dealt a heavy blow to the Workers’ Party (PT) and, more broadly, to the cause of democracy in Latin America. In 2022, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished some six million votes ahead of Jair Bolsonaro in the first round, a margin that narrowed to about two million in the runoff. This time, Flávio Bolsonaro finished 2.2 million votes ahead of Lula, a lead of three percentage points. That makes the second round on October 25 especially difficult for Lula and the Brazilian left. The candidates who finished behind the top two, who together took around six million votes (roughly 6 percent), are all on the far right. They supported Jair Bolsonaro’s government and opposed Lula’s, so a broad front is likely to form against him in the runoff. There is a real chance that the Bolsonaro family will return to the presidency. Right-Wing Momentum The same dynamic shaped the legislative races. In the Senate, Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party (PL) grew from fifteen seats to twenty-eight, while the PT held steady at nine (out of eighty-one in total). Hopes for a larger female presence in Congress also went unrealized. The gubernatorial races told a similar story. Sergio Moro, the far-right senator who jailed Lula in the wake of the parliamentary and judicial coup against Dilma Rousseff, won the governorship of Paraná in the first round. The far right also won outright in wealthy states like Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul. In the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil’s lower house, the PT fared especially badly in São Paulo state, where veteran party figures such as Paulo Teixeira, Nabil Bonduki, and José Dirceu failed to win seats. The PT’s top candidate in the state, Luana Zaratini, received 230,000 votes, while the PL’s top candidate, Luciano Pavanato, received three million. Nationally, the left-wing parties with parliamentary representation — the PT, the Party of Socialism and Liberty, Rede, and the Communist Party — grew from eighty-eight deputies to ninety-six. But they were outpaced by Bolsonaro’s PL, which jumped from ninety-nine to 120 (out of 513 in total). When Bolsonaro was first elected, in 2018, the general mood was one of revolt. The far right rode into office on an enthusiastic movement from below, one that filled the streets. This has not happened with Flávio this year. Despite the PL’s electoral success and the strength of Bolsonarismo in the ballot box, the streets are lukewarm. The promises sound less like a plan to overturn everything, as in the previous campaign, and more like one to resume the Right’s unfinished work, especially amnesty for the family and revenge against the Supreme Court. The movement now coming from above might be more dangerous than the one coming from below. American Interference Contrary to expectations, US intervention did not take the form of noisy meddling by Donald Trump and his allies. It appears to have come instead through effective background pressure on the Federal Police and the Supreme Court, which became the center of the political debate. This proved particularly damaging. Rather than debating questions of policy and program, the campaign revolved around corruption, the far right’s favorite terrain. And this time, the debate centered more on the Supreme Court than on the presidency. The first thing Washington did after Jair Bolsonaro’s arrest was to apply the Magnitsky Act, imposing sanctions on the magistrate responsible for the case, Alexandre de Moraes, to punish him for going after Trump’s main ally on the continent. The pressure on the Brazilian judicial system has continued ever since, less visibly but with greater aggression. The court’s own conduct made it an easy target. Its justices have a record of protecting bourgeois interests, and the line between public and private affairs is poorly drawn: justices commonly become multimillionaire lawyers once they leave the bench. This is the story of the Banco Master scandal. Judges and, above all, their relatives were tied to multimillion-dollar contracts, favors, gifts, and Epstein-style parties organized by the fraudulent banker at the center of the biggest financial crime in Brazil’s history. Among them was Moraes’s wife, Viviane Moraes. Five of the court’s eleven justices were implicated, yet the crisis revolved around Moraes, and the far right used it to attack the figure who had put Bolsonaro behind bars. The key question about the revelation of Viviane Moraes’s secret deals is how Justice André Mendonça, a far-right evangelical preacher with close ties to the US evangelical right, got access to the confidential documents. The manner, the speed, and the access enjoyed by this Bolsonaro appointee strongly suggest that there was US interference in the process. During a heated Supreme Court session broadcast live on television one month before the vote, Moraes said the report had been drafted in a time frame of seventy-two hours and insisted that time frame was impossible for a document of that kind. According to him, the metadata proved the report had not been produced by the Federal Police at all but by outside agents, likely foreigners, who simply handed the final product to the police. The metadata, Moraes insisted, showed that the police inquiry was opened and closed on the same day on a Federal Police computer, meaning the report had merely been inserted into it. He described this as evidence of attempted foreign interference in Brazil’s elections. Mendonça also intervened during the offensive against Moraes by ousting the chief of the Federal Police, whom Lula had appointed and who had been responsible for containing the January 8, 2023 coup attempt. Probable US intervention in the controversy over the Supreme Court shifted the terms of the debate to the advantage of the Brazilian right, in contrast with the punitive tariffs Trump imposed after Bolsonaro’s imprisonment that merely increased support for Lula. This time, the focus was not on the action taken by the Trump administration but on the allegations of corruption among judges who had backed the Lula government. A Weak Government While the focus on the Supreme Court certainly made things easier for Bolsonaro, it is impossible to ignore the fact that Lula’s third government has been the least transformative of his three terms. This is partly explained by how Brazil’s institutions have evolved since the coup against his successor, Dilma Rousseff. The coup against Dilma was both a coup by parliament and a coup for parliament. The conservative right in Congress toppled her to install one of its own leading figures, Vice President Michel Temer, in the presidency. At the same time, it also sought to weaken the executive and strengthen the legislature, while the process also empowered the Supreme Court at the presidency’s expense. As a result of these efforts, Lula’s ability to govern has been greatly restricted and depends far more on Congress, including on matters like the budget. Under Bolsonaro, Congress took a direct institutional hand in writing the budget and directing public spending autonomously, in a way never seen before, and that practice has continued under Lula. According to political scientist André Singer, Brazil has moved from a presidential system built on broad parliamentary coalitions to something closer to a semi-presidential postcoup regime. But the weakening of the presidency does not in itself explain why the PT did so poorly. The government has relatively little to show in terms of improving the lives of the working class. It is true that unemployment is lower than ever, while levels of hunger have been reduced to the benchmark of Lula’s earlier governments, after rising sharply under Temer and (especially) Bolsonaro . But while life has largely returned to its pre-pandemic form, conditions remain very hard for working people. In the final Quaest poll before the election, voters in households earning up to twice the minimum wage (about US$620 a month) backed Lula over Flávio by 52 percent to 23 percent. That group has seen life improve as extreme poverty fell after the pandemic. However, this was not enough to offset the PT’s losses elsewhere. Among households earning two to five times the minimum wage, Flávio led narrowly by 36 percent to 35 percent. Among those earning more than five times, he led by a wider margin, 42 percent to 30 percent. While hunger has fallen, food prices have continued to rise, albeit to a lesser extent than under Bolsonaro. The quality of food has declined, with more semi-industrial products and higher prices for meat and other staples that were far more accessible before COVID-19. The availability of meat matters in particular: it played a central role in Lula’s 2022 campaign. Employment tells a similar story. Unemployment is down, but work has become harder. Temer’s administration stripped away a series of labor rights, and none of those rights has been restored under Lula. Jobs under PJ ( pessoa jurídica ) contracts, which cover individual freelancers and sole proprietors, have grown at the expense of formal employment, bringing far greater insecurity. Much of the job growth has come in service sectors tied to apps and digital platforms, where poor conditions and a lack of protections have made life worse. Debt Debt is a particular problem. Working-class indebtedness has grown, and this is especially relevant for the PT and for Lula, because the party’s governmental strategy has been to expand the capacity of families to take on debt. When it came to transport, for example, the main strategy was to widen access to car purchases through credit, rather than invest heavily in public transit. There was a huge expansion of access to housing for those earning one to five times the minimum wage. But almost all of it came from subsidizing private housing through the Minha Casa, Minha Vida program, which widened access by pushing people into debt. Public universities expanded, but the largest growth was in private institutions, through grants and financing schemes that also meant taking on more debt. In other words, the gains of the Lula and Dilma governments rested on greater access to goods like cars, housing, and education, bought with increased household debt. More than two decades after the launch of policies that sought to integrate the working class into mass society through consumption, 80 percent of families now carry high levels of debt. The Left and the Mass Movements Efforts to avoid conflict with Congress, the Supreme Court, and Brazil’s capitalist class also made it harder for Lula’s government to deliver on its campaign pledges. While devastation of the Amazon jungle was reduced, Lula made drilling for oil off the mouth of the Amazon River one of his priorities after taking office, posing a serious risk of spills along the Amazonian coast. His government also announced a plan that would have placed strategic stretches of the Madeira, Tapajós, and Tocantins rivers in the National Privatization Program, with the aim of turning them into export corridors for soybeans. It was mobilization by indigenous and student movements during the COP30 protests in Belém do Pará that stopped the project. The early supporters of this abortive scheme included Guilherme Boulos, the minister in charge of the presidential general secretariat and relations with social movements, and Sônia Guajajara, the minister of indigenous peoples. Guajajara won 160,000 votes in the 2022 elections; this time, she received just 54,000. Most telling was the government’s failure, or unwillingness, to convert workers’ struggles into mobilizations in its favor. The central working-class demand since Lula’s election has been for an end to the 6x1 schedule (six days of work followed by one day off) and a reduction of the working week. However, the PT channeled this demand into a purely parliamentary fight with no strikes or street protests to back it up. The same demobilizing logic applied to the app workers’ strike (the breque dos apps ), perhaps the most explosive moment of working-class struggle in São Paulo during recent years. While the government moved to head off the strike, the only proposal it offered these workers was credit to buy bicycles. Foreign Policy In terms of foreign policy, Lula’s government never developed a coherent line of opposition to the policies of the Trump administration. It did not follow through on threats to directly tax American goods and preferred to negotiate with Washington over its invocation of the Magnitsky Act. In relation to Palestine, Lula did put forward an early condemnation of Israel’s genocide, and his government joined South Africa’s genocide case at the International Court of Justice last year. However, the administration also used the human rights ministry to counterbalance its relationship with Tel Aviv. Silvio de Almeida, the human rights minister who left the post amid sexual harassment allegations, refused for months to condemn the genocide, saying it was a matter for the president and the foreign ministry. His successor, Macaé Evaristo, steered the ministry toward a policy of “combating antisemitism” that involved visiting Jewish institutions, the Holocaust museum, and pro-Zionist synagogues while ignoring the Palestinian community and taking no stand against Islamophobia. The government’s response to the failed Bolsonarist coup was also inadequate. It supported the Supreme Court while it declined to pursue important targets such as the Argentine Fernando Cerimedo , who is linked to US and Israeli interference networks in Latin America and was removed from the attorney general’s final indictment, and Jovem Pan, the major media outlet that called for the coup attempt. Winning the Runoff Lula’s most popular moves in the run-up to the election involved changing his administration’s previous positions on those issues. His government had previously tried only to regulate the growth of online betting, which has hit working-class households hard, football betting above all. Now it moved to ban it altogether. Payments under the Bolsa Família scheme, designed to reduce poverty and extreme hunger, had not been increased to take account of inflation over the previous three years. This changed on the eve of the vote. The government also began investing in public health against obesity by buying treatments such as Mounjaro, having previously failed to do so. These policy shifts boosted support for Lula and may even have prevented Flávio Bolsonaro from winning outright in the first round. If Lula is to be reelected in the runoff, he has to generate hope of change. This has been the central problem of the Brazilian left. Banks, big business, most politicians, and most of the media lean to the right, yet the prevailing perception is that Brazil lives under a left-wing regime, and that the Bolsonaro camp is the alternative to the status quo. Lula has not managed to show that he, rather than the far right, represents change. That is partly because his administration has not been a government of change. Abstentions, blank votes, and spoiled ballots together reached 24 percent of the electorate. The rate of abstention alone was 21 percent, the highest since 1998. For the PT to win over even some former right-wing and anti-regime voters, and to build a social base of its own instead of watching it abstain, it will need a more combative strategy built on popular and social mobilization. That is the only way to defeat the far right.
